Together they owned a property-development company in Yokohama, placing him within a family enterprise whose work was rooted in the city's real-estate market. The surviving accounts do not name the company or distinguish each brother's management responsibilities.

Isaka's public footprint is otherwise unusually small. No dependable chronology describes the firm's projects, its scale or what became of his interest after the early 1990s. That absence limits a fuller account of how he worked or how the business evolved. What can be stated with confidence is narrower: he was a Japanese co-owner of a Yokohama family property-development business.
